20261023c 为正式新版镜像：DXL 2.0 IMU 兼容已接入实际运动主程序和标定流程，默认自动识别支持的总线格式，Studio 显示实际识别结果。

补充兼容核验（2026-10-23）：已核对 [ScrapMeta 的 imu_to_dxl 固件](https://github.com/ScrapMeta/microduck-diy/tree/db04d323caa053ae0c96629268392cdbe7dc8b4f/imu_to_dxl/firmware)。其默认 DXL2 / ID 200 / 1 Mbps / 124-12 数据格式已由本版现有运行程序支持；对方真实 C 协议实现与本版 Rust 读取路径的 7 项串口仿真核验通过。小板需预先刷好与实板匹配的固件，镜像不会自动刷写 MCU；真实小板验收仍待进行。本次补充兼容说明，镜像附件和校验值保持原样。

## 本版内容

- **Feetech 总线 IMU**：识别 FT6、兼容的 IMU-to-DXL Feetech 固件，保留原来的数据格式和回复顺序。
- **DXL 2.0 总线 IMU**：支持 ID 200、124/12 SFLP 数据布局。IMU 和 15 颗 Feetech 舵机由同一个程序依次查询，共用采集时限。
- **默认自动识别**；也可在 `[bus]` 中用 `imu_protocol = "feetech"` 或 `"dxl2"` 固定协议。探测不修改芯片 ID、波特率或 EEPROM。
- **换协议后重新校准**：旧 Feetech 的安装方向确认不能直接授权 DXL2 上力。Studio 会清除不再适用的采集结果，小助手保留实际协议绑定；重新标定和恢复流程仍可使用。
- **显示真实信息**：页面区分协议、布局及身份；DXL2 没提供的芯片计数器、状态位和芯片侧数据年龄不编造数值。
- 保留 I²C BNO08x / LSM6DSV16X、初次站姿采数、IMU 重新标定、模型管理与传感器页面。模型和其他 daemon 沿用已核验版本。

支持的是上述协议和数据布局，**不是所有厂家的任意 IMU 固件**。其他寄存器格式、ID、波特率需要适配。更换物理模块或安装方向后，即使协议相同也应重新校准。

## 验证范围

- Studio 最终功能版本完整测试共运行 1,037 项，4 项跳过，其余通过；其中协议相关的后端、小助手和浏览器回归 151 项通过。
- 控制核心 251 项、参数 110 项、单实例/更新健康门控集成测试 18 项通过；包含 19 项 DXL2 与混合串口测试。
- robotd 单元测试逐项独立运行：新版 296 项通过、2 项跳过、17 项失败；原提交相同条件下有相同的 17 项失败，没有新增失败。新增 DXL2 完整标定及故障停止流程通过。
- 镜像脚本 117 项在 Linux root 下通过；交付文件完成 SHA256、xz、独立解压、分区和 ext4 只读检查，核对实际 robotd、Studio、小助手及出厂状态。
- **新增总线兼容尚待真板验收**，没有连接或修改你的鸭子。摄像头默认仍为测试画面，按硬件自动启停摄像头/ToF 服务未在本次实现。

## 下载和源码

适用于 **Radxa Zero 3W + 飞特 HD-1910**。下载 `.img.xz` 与同名 `.sha256`，核对后烧录到空白或已备份的 TF 卡。开机连接鸭子热点，打开 `http://10.42.0.1:8000/`，按上手清单操作。

- 镜像：`microduck-replica-20261023c.img.xz`，712,068,864 字节。
- SHA256：`10009c0a4aa963900719649836f5544036ad52cc15e3a0228eef05f6b747dab5`。
- Studio / 镜像冻结源码：`dd7a753026c40b0bf385374a896e7253cff42720`。
- [runtime 源码](https://github.com/fanhao375/Microduck-kissqy/tree/0791fcd44f71c705dc8bb0fbcde405593b52d19b)：`0791fcd44f71c705dc8bb0fbcde405593b52d19b`，build `4734cbb-feetech-imu-auto-control.44`。
- robotd SHA256：`edf182edb7bf11aeeeedfdab98170ab2ec48a9ec18417f9b68c744b0a60c6d16`；小助手 0.7.1。
- 附件六份：镜像、校验值、manifest、licenses、third-party、models。

record.body: That's a completely different class of robot. The Beni robot is just a toy, it's just connect the app and drive it around, record videos and do some fancy tricks like flips. Train it yourself, write software, hack it, etc. It depends what you're trying to get for your daughter. Is it something to get her into robotics? Then probably the Microduck is the way. If it's literally just a toy, then the Beni robot is better because that's literally all it is.

record.author: kodoman
record.body: I guess we are really debating the semantics of the sentences now like lawyers but to me the verb show is not particularly difficult to achieve or ambitious or misleading to use in this sort of product. A toy with a that has a smiley face and a frowning face is capable of showing two different emotions. Your second one point also does not seem like a lie to me since it's claiming to emulate natural ingredient (although here I guess to be just like means to emulate perfectly). I don't really see why any one would look at the product and it's marketing as evil. It seems to me aimed at people who can not have pets and are want to create a simulation of a soothing positive interaction with a pet. I don't see this as exploitative (apart from it's exploiting a desire that people have in the same way that virtually all products do), I can not see someone forming a relationship with this to the detriment of human interaction or exacerbate some kind of mental illness or cause addiction. It does seem a little expensive and that would be my only criticism of the product so far as I can see.

record.author: EvanAnderson
record.body: > I have no interest in a relationship with a robot. I think I could, if it meant I could keep the experience of having a pet. I've had cats going back to my twenties. I dearly love my fifteen y/o cat. She's my last cat, though. As I approach fifty I've grown tired of hefting bags of litter and food, stooping to clean up after her, taking her to the vet, and administering her medication. When she's finally dead (which is hopefully not for a good long time) I'm not going to get another. This makes me really sad. I'll miss having a cat around. As I age, though, I don't want the encumbrance of taking care of a pet, nor do I want to cause hardship to family if I suddenly become unable to care for a pet (dying, being hospitalized, living arrangement changes and owning a pet isn't allowed, etc). If there was a robot alternative I'd jump on it. I think my brain would adjust fine to a convincingly-executed robotic cat. Our brains instinctively ascribe agency to objects moving in non-inertial frames, for example. Think about all the people who name their Roomba, install googly eyes on it, etc. People easily accept inanimate objects that behave like living things, to the point of developing feelings for them. When my cat is gone I hope to get the opportunity to choose a "relationship" with a convincing robotic cat versus not having one at all. I wouldn't expect everyone to feel this way. I certainly don't want to legislate away pet ownership. I bet that, if good robotic pets become available, we'll see a significant number of people favoring them over living pets for convenience, long-term cost, freedom from anxiety about the pet's health and eventual death, and the opportunity for companionship in living arrangements where pets aren't allowed. I've said, for years, that I think there's hundreds of billions of dollars for the company who can make really good robotic pets. If somebody can get the "soft robotics" down and build / train good animal behavior models I think they'll be able to print money.

If there was a robot alternative I'd jump on it. I think my brain would adjust fine to a convincingly-executed robotic cat. Our brains instinctively ascribe agency to objects moving in non-inertial frames, for example. Think about all the people who name their Roomba, install googly eyes on it, etc. People easily accept inanimate objects that behave like living things, to the point of developing feelings for them.

When my cat is gone I hope to get the opportunity to choose a "relationship" with a convincing robotic cat versus not having one at all.

I wouldn't expect everyone to feel this way. I certainly don't want to legislate away pet ownership.

I bet that, if good robotic pets become available, we'll see a significant number of people favoring them over living pets for convenience, long-term cost, freedom from anxiety about the pet's health and eventual death, and the opportunity for companionship in living arrangements where pets aren't allowed.

I've said, for years, that I think there's hundreds of billions of dollars for the company who can make really good robotic pets. If somebody can get the "soft robotics" down and build / train good animal behavior models I think they'll be able to print money.

record.author: elBoberido
record.body: iceoryx2 maintainer here. Of course everybody has different requirements when it comes to IPC and if a rich set of supported languages is the highest priority, then protocols like JSONRPC are a good option. But using such protocols for local IPC also has downsides, especially when the amount of data increases and the available resources are limited. This is where iceoryx2 has its strengths by utilizing shared memory for communication. We also split up the data flow from the control flow and one could send data to other processes without a context switch, in a way similar to what io_uring is doing. There is an upcoming blog post where we describe the possibilities shared memory enables compared to using sockets. I'll post it here once it is published. Like another poster already commented, while iceoryx2 is implemented in Rust, it already support other languages, like C, C++, C# and Python. We'd love to add even more languages to the list, with Go being on top of our wishlist, but like always with OSS, someone needs to do the work or needs to step up and fund the work.

record.author: kodoman
record.body: Second that it's unlikely that Plato agrees with Socrates on writing in the Phaedrus. When reading Plato you should think of him as writing dialogues for people to see various arguments and arguments develop over the books, for example Timaeus goes against positions held by Socrates and even more so later in the Parmenides. Plato is not linear either and if you really want to understand what Plato held you have to look at what the academy taught and what the Platonism became. Though clearly Platonism develops and changes and has various different flavors that academics pick out such as middle-platonism and neo-platonism. I would say it's not definite what Plato believed and one might say that he entertained multiple ideas at the same time, though clearly despised many positions.

record.author: tamimio
record.body: Because ROS sucks. If you have ever had the chance to work with it, you will know, here’s a heads-up/recap on why: - multiple configs all over: xml, cmake, yaml, “””launch file”””, urdf, and others, im not joking, those are all configs! - you might have a node running but it’s technically not? The mystery mostly that the node isn’t publishing, why? Well, there are gazillions of reasons, maybe qos mismatch, wrong topic name space, timestamp issues, frame ID, etc etc - the debugging is distributed, so a failure you see (assuming you found it anyway), it could be actually from another process, interface, driver, you name it. - so many dependencies, you have ros itself, then ubuntu, then gazebo, python, other libraries needed to build, so you could spend a whole week troubleshooting just because one of these mismatch something else. - ros1 sucked, look it up, realtime limitation, security, discovery, tooling etc, so they made ros2, supposedly better, but the unnecessary complexity added is abysmal, dds, qos profile, call back groups, lifecycle nodes, and other cluster fuck of stuff. - you have also with implied status, so different terminals can and will behave differently, you got sourced workspaces, environment variables, automatic discovery, overlay order and others, can work in one terminal setup but not in another. - a lot of packages were done for specific robot or by a student who was doing some school work, that package will not just work on the same set up you have, I have seen robots of the same model and the package won’t work because the motor driver is slightly different. Also, that package is mostly abandoned anyway. And you have all the security concerns with all that stuff above, that’s why it never gets added to the same network where serious automation things are happening, in fact, I have never ever seen ROS used in real commercial products, for good. First time I got to work with it I thought it’s just me, so I ended up building the drone platform from scratch in much easier and simpler way, only to find most of the industry share the same idea. I can rant more but my take away, if you can do something without it, do it, don’t try to rely on it, it’s like 100x worse than kubernetes, once you are fully invested in it and building everything around it, it will be hard to replace.

raw_text:
Because ROS sucks. If you have ever had the chance to work with it, you will know, here’s a heads-up/recap on why:

- multiple configs all over: xml, cmake, yaml, “””launch file”””, urdf, and others, im not joking, those are all configs!

- you might have a node running but it’s technically not? The mystery mostly that the node isn’t publishing, why? Well, there are gazillions of reasons, maybe qos mismatch, wrong topic name space, timestamp issues, frame ID, etc etc

- the debugging is distributed, so a failure you see (assuming you found it anyway), it could be actually from another process, interface, driver, you name it.

- so many dependencies, you have ros itself, then ubuntu, then gazebo, python, other libraries needed to build, so you could spend a whole week troubleshooting just because one of these mismatch something else.

- ros1 sucked, look it up, realtime limitation, security, discovery, tooling etc, so they made ros2, supposedly better, but the unnecessary complexity added is abysmal, dds, qos profile, call back groups, lifecycle nodes, and other cluster fuck of stuff.

- you have also with implied status, so different terminals can and will behave differently, you got sourced workspaces, environment variables, automatic discovery, overlay order and others, can work in one terminal setup but not in another.

- a lot of packages were done for specific robot or by a student who was doing some school work, that package will not just work on the same set up you have, I have seen robots of the same model and the package won’t work because the motor driver is slightly different. Also, that package is mostly abandoned anyway.

And you have all the security concerns with all that stuff above, that’s why it never gets added to the same network where serious automation things are happening, in fact, I have never ever seen ROS used in real commercial products, for good.

First time I got to work with it I thought it’s just me, so I ended up building the drone platform from scratch in much easier and simpler way, only to find most of the industry share the same idea.

I can rant more but my take away, if you can do something without it, do it, don’t try to rely on it, it’s like 100x worse than kubernetes, once you are fully invested in it and building everything around it, it will be hard to replace.

record.body:
---
title: MicroDuck TinyVLA
emoji: 🐤
colorFrom: yellow
colorTo: gray
sdk: docker
app_port: 8080
pinned: false
models:
  - AlexWortega/tinyvla-microduck-stage25
---

# MicroDuck TinyVLA Space

TinyVLA controls a live MicroDuck MuJoCo simulation from a 256×256 robot
head-camera frame, the exact 61-dimensional policy state, and a language
instruction. Physics and rendering run in the browser; model inference runs on
the Space CPU.

The backend is fully ONNX Runtime CPU inference. The checkpoint is split into
`vision.onnx`, a cacheable `semantic.onnx`, and an `action.onnx` containing all
10 flow-matching denoise steps. The CPU bundle dynamically quantizes vision and
semantic weights to INT8; the sensitive flow sampler remains FP32.
PyTorch, Transformers and LeRobot are not installed in the Space image.

The client follows the Stage 2.5 serving contract exactly:

- simulate controls at 50 Hz;
- capture a fresh head-camera observation every five controls (10 Hz);
- request a `100×14` raw joint-offset chunk;
- execute only its first five rows;
- apply each row as `DEFAULT_POSE + offset`, then replan.

The preset programs reproduce the 13D command schedules used for Stage 2.5
training. A Custom program is also available, but deliberately sends an all-zero
13D command; arbitrary language outside the training distribution may not work.

## Space configuration

The deployed Space uses free `cpu-basic` hardware (2 vCPU, 16 GB RAM). The
vision encoder runs once per request. The language/semantic graph runs only
when the instruction changes or every 50 control steps; its 8-token output is
cached between requests.

Variables:

| Name | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `MODEL_REPO_ID` | `AlexWortega/tinyvla-microduck-stage25` | Hub model repository |
| `MODEL_REVISION` | unset | Optional immutable model revision |
| `MODEL_PATH` | unset | Local/attached model directory; bypasses Hub download |
| `VLA_MAX_SESSIONS` | `8` | LRU limit for per-tab semantic caches |
| `EXPECTED_ACTION_HORIZON` | `100` | Reject a non-Stage-2.5 checkpoint at startup |
| `VLA_ONNX_SUBDIR` | `onnx/cpu` | CPU-optimized ONNX bundle within the mounted model repo |
| `ORT_INTRA_OP_THREADS` | auto (up to `2`) | ONNX Runtime CPU threads |

For this deployment the private model repository is attached read-only at
`/model`, with `MODEL_PATH=/model`. This avoids copying an access token into the
container. If a volume is not available, use `HF_TOKEN` as a Space secret with
read access; never commit a token to either repository.

The model directory must contain the exported bundle:

```text
onnx/
  cpu/
    metadata.json
    microduck_normalization.json
    tokenizer/tokenizer.json
    vision.onnx
    vision.onnx.data
    semantic.onnx
    semantic.onnx.data
    action.onnx
    action.onnx.data
```

The original `model.safetensors` can remain in the repository for provenance,
but the Space neither maps nor loads it. No Qwen files are fetched at startup.

The existing `AlexWortega/tinyvla-microduck` main revision is the earlier
50-action checkpoint. Do not point this Space at it: startup validates a
100-action horizon and fails visibly instead of silently serving the wrong VLA.
Publish `artifacts/tinyvla-microduck-stage25` to the default repository above,
or set `MODEL_REPO_ID`/`MODEL_REVISION` to another location containing the same
Stage 2.5 bundle.

From the OpenDuck repository root, the non-destructive new-repository path is:

```bash
hf repos create AlexWortega/tinyvla-microduck-stage25 --type model --private
hf upload-large-folder AlexWortega/tinyvla-microduck-stage25 \
  artifacts/tinyvla-microduck-stage25 --repo-type model \
  --exclude '**/__pycache__/**' --exclude '**/*.pyc'
```

## Deploy

Create an empty Docker Space, then upload this directory as its repository root:

```bash
cd spaces/microduck-vla
hf upload-large-folder YOUR_NAME/YOUR_SPACE . --repo-type space
```

Every push rebuilds and restarts the Space. ONNX sessions load after the web
server starts, and the in-app BIOS shows `TINYVLA [LOADING]` until all three are
ready. `GET /health` reports `engine: onnxruntime` when the new backend is live.

## Run locally

```bash
docker build -t microduck-vla .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 \
  -e MODEL_PATH=/model \
  -v /absolute/path/to/tinyvla-microduck:/model:ro \
  microduck-vla
```

For frontend-only development, run the API on port 8080 and Vite on 5173:

```bash
cd app
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## API

- `GET /api/health` (also `/health`)
- `POST /api/reset` (also `/reset`)
- `POST /api/predict` (also `/predict`)
- interactive schema at `/api/docs`

`session_id` is optional for compatibility, but the browser sends one UUID per
tab. The backend keeps a single model and swaps only the small language
semantic/recovery cache per session, preventing visitors from contaminating one
another's control state.

## Provenance and safety

The browser simulator is adapted from
[`pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator`](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator)
at revision `1261013e7e28ba2a6878bd76ae573751c0e4b457`. MicroDuck policies and
robot sources are Apache-2.0 upstream. The included 3D assets carry the upstream
CC BY-NC-SA/non-commercial terms disclosed by the OpenDuck dataset/model card;
preserve attribution and verify the terms before redistribution.

The Stage 2.5 checkpoint is experimental. A browser simulation is not a hardware
safety validation. On a physical robot, retain joint/current limits and an
independent emergency stop.

# Microduck Playground Competition

A browser-based MuJoCo racing game for three Microduck robots. Each duck runs
its own local physics simulation and locomotion policy in the browser. Pick a
winner, watch the ducks complete two laps around an oval playground, and earn
or lose fish according to your prediction.

The game is a front-end application: MuJoCo runs through WebAssembly and
`onnxruntime-web` evaluates the trained ONNX policies locally. There is no
Python server, inference API, database, or multiplayer backend required.

## Game rules

1. The game opens with a betting screen. The player starts with one fish and
   chooses Duck 1, Duck 2, or Duck 3.
2. All three ducks start from the same start/finish line on equivalent lanes.
   Their lanes have the same route length; the first duck is not placed ahead.
3. The ducks race in rollers mode by default. Press `M` to switch all three
   racers between rollers and feet.
4. The first duck to complete two laps reaches the winner podium. Standing on
   the podium ends the race and opens the settlement screen.
5. A correct bet awards one fish. A wrong bet removes one fish. The result is
   shown in a large animated settlement panel, together with the winner and
   the live race statistics.
6. Press `Space` after settlement to start the next round. Each round resets
   the three racers to the same start line while the fish balance remains.
7. A fallen duck is handled independently. The stand-up policy is called for
   that duck, which then resumes from its current track position. A recovery
   failure only affects that racer; it does not restart the whole game or reset
   the other ducks.

## What is visible during a race

- Three visually distinct racers: charcoal, purple, and red.
- A labelled `START / FINISH` line.
- Bright route beacons marking the navigation waypoints.
- A live scoreboard with each duck's colour, lap count, distance, and speed.
- The current fish balance and the selected bet.
- A winner podium and an animated win/loss settlement screen.

## Locomotion policies

The application loads the policies lazily from `app/public/policies/` and
uses the same policy interface as the official Microduck runtime.

| Action | Policy | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walk | `BEST_alpha_walking.onnx` | Velocity-tracking walking policy |
| Stand up | `BEST_alpha_stand.onnx` | Recovers a fallen duck |
| Sit / stand | `BEST_alpha_sitstand.onnx` | Sit and stand action |
| Roller drive | `BEST_roller.onnx` | Velocity-tracking four-wheel locomotion |
| Roller crouch | `BEST_roller_crouch.onnx` | Crouch-glide action |
| Roll | `roulade.onnx` | Roll action and recovery |
| Ground pick | `alpha_ground_pick.onnx` | Ground-pick action |
| Kick | `ball_kick_left.onnx`, `ball_kick_right.onnx` | Leg-mode kick actions |

## Controls

- `M`: switch all racers between feet and rollers
- Arrow keys / `WASD` / `ZQSD`: manually control the hero duck
- `Q` / `E`: left / right kick in feet mode
- `F`: alternate kick in feet mode
- `R`: sit/stand in feet mode, crouch-glide in rollers mode
- `G`: ground pick in feet mode
- `C`: toggle the chase camera
- Mouse drag: orbit the camera
- Mouse wheel: zoom
- `Space`: reset from the title/pause state, or start the next round after settlement

Keyboard input takes control of the hero duck. Releasing the movement keys
returns it to the oval route controller. A connected gamepad is also
supported.

## Local installation

Conda is not required. Node.js and npm are enough; they may be installed in
the normal macOS user environment or managed with `nvm`.

Node.js 22+ is recommended. The current `package-lock.json` should be used so
that every installation gets the same dependency versions.

```bash
git clone https://huggingface.co/spaces/HandsomeWu666/Microduck-playground-competition.git
cd Microduck-playground-competition

# Required when cloning the repository's large model and mesh files.
git lfs install
git lfs pull

cd app
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:5173>. For a production build:

```bash
cd app
npm run build
npm run preview
```

The ONNX policies, MJCF files, meshes, audio, and scene assets are served
from `app/public/`. If Git LFS is unavailable, the large files may remain as
small pointer files and the simulator will fail while loading the model or
policy. On macOS, install Git LFS first, for example with `brew install git-lfs`.

## Hugging Face Spaces deployment

Choose **Static** as the Space SDK. This project produces a static Vite
bundle and does not need Gradio, Python, GPU hardware, or a long-running
Docker process. The repository includes the prebuilt bundle at the repository
root, so
the Space only serves static files and does not need a cloud build step.

```yaml
sdk: static
app_file: index.html
```

On the Space creation page, select:

- License: `Apache-2.0` (with third-party components retaining their upstream
  licenses)
- Space SDK: `Static`
- Hardware: the free/default option; physics and policy inference run in the
  visitor's browser
- Storage bucket: not needed

The existing `Dockerfile` is kept as an optional fallback for environments
that require the Docker SDK. When source code changes, rebuild locally with
`cd app && npm ci && npm run build`, then refresh the checked-in root bundle
(`index.html`, `bundle/`, `assets/`, `policies/`, and `robot/`) before pushing a
new Space revision.

## Architecture

The project combines React, MUI, React Three Fiber, MuJoCo, and ONNX Runtime:

- `app/src/game/game.js` owns the simulation loop, policy sessions, MuJoCo
  models/data, race state, lap counting, winner handling, and fall recovery.
- `app/src/game/oval-track.js` defines the oval track, equal-length lanes,
  route waypoints, route beacons, start/finish marker, and winner podium.
- `app/src/store.js` stores the game phase, bet, fish balance, locomotion mode,
  racer progress, and settlement state.
- `app/src/ui/Hud.jsx` renders the betting screen, scoreboard, fish display,
  race status, and settlement animation.
- `app/src/game/variants.js` defines the duck colour variants and locomotion
  assets.

Each racer owns an independent MuJoCo model/data pair and policy session. A
failure or recovery of one racer therefore does not restart the other racers.

## References and attribution

This project is an experimental racing extension of the official Microduck
browser environment. It reuses the official robot assets, MJCF/kinematics
layout, and ONNX policy contract while adding the local three-duck oval race,
betting, fish economy, scoreboard, recovery flow, and podium ceremony.

- Official simulator environment:
  [pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator)
- Official robot model and assets:
  [pollen-robotics/microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck)
- Official reinforcement-learning policies and inference contract:
  [pollen-robotics/microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl)
- Earlier family-race reference Space:
  [Nirav-Madhani/microduck-racer](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Nirav-Madhani/microduck-racer)

Please check the upstream repositories for their individual asset, model, and
software license terms. The bundled `zzfx` audio utility is distributed under
its MIT license.

## License

The Space is marked Apache-2.0 for the project distribution. Third-party
dependencies, robot assets, trained policies, and upstream code remain subject
to their respective licenses and attribution requirements listed above.

record.body:
---
title: Microduck Arena
emoji: 🦆
colorFrom: gray
colorTo: yellow
sdk: docker
app_port: 7860
pinned: false
short_description: Race Microduck policies on a clock you can trust
thumbnail: https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-arena/resolve/main/docs/thumbnail.png
hf_oauth: true
---

# microduck-arena

Race a Microduck policy against every other policy, on a clock you can trust.

New to competing? Read [Train your first policy](docs/guides/train-a-policy.md),
then open **Training & rules** on your chosen challenge.

Submitted policies are evaluated **server-side** on a fixed course over five
perturbed seeds, at every commanded speed in the event's declared sweep, and the
best result is recorded. A time reported by a browser is a number in devtools;
this one reproduces on the Space's hardware (x86_64 Linux), and you can download
any published policy and race it yourself. Elsewhere — a Mac, or another
architecture — the same run gives different numbers: the servo model is chaotic
enough that a run diverges after a few seconds of simulated time, so a local time
is indicative, not the board's.

It runs two ways, and both are first-class:

- **Locally**, with no Hugging Face account, no OAuth and no network. The run log
  is a directory on your disk.
- **As a Space** (this repo is one). Same code path; its times are the
  board's, and a local run on other hardware gives indicative ones.

## Deploying to the Space

The source of truth is the GitHub repo
[`pollen-robotics/microduck-arena`](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck-arena).
**Every push to `main` deploys** — `.github/workflows/deploy-space.yml` publishes
the tree to <https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-arena>.

`git push` to the Hub does not work here: it rejects binary files pushed through
plain git and asks for Xet instead, and this repo vendors a GLB, forty-odd STLs
and an ONNX policy. So the deploy goes through the Hub API, which speaks Xet
natively — the same script the workflow runs is the one to run by hand:

```bash
uv run python scripts/deploy_space.py            # publishes the working tree
uv run python scripts/deploy_space.py --dry-run  # shows what would go
```

The run log is not part of this. It lives in the `ARENA_DATASET` dataset repo,
which a deploy never touches, so the board and the standings survive every
redeploy — see *Running as a Space* below.

The Space rebuilds itself on each upload. Its own Docker build re-measures the
golden run and fails if the physics does not reproduce, so a broken build is
better than a silently wrong leaderboard.

## Releasing

A tag `vX.Y.Z` matching `version` in `pyproject.toml` builds the wheel — package, built site,
meshes — and attaches it to a GitHub release (`.github/workflows/release.yml`). That wheel is
what `microduck-challenges` depends on:

```bash
git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0
```

## Running as a Space

The container filesystem is ephemeral, so a Space needs somewhere durable to
keep the run log. Set two things in **Settings → Variables and secrets**:

| name | kind | value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ARENA_DATASET` | variable | the dataset repo that holds the log, e.g. `pollen-robotics/microduck-arena-runs` |
| `HF_TOKEN` | **secret** | a token with write access to that dataset |

Without both, the Space still boots and the board still works — but every
recorded run is lost the next time it restarts or wakes from sleep. A
published policy's `.onnx` is not at risk from this: it lives in the
publishing author's own Hub repo, not on the Space. `GET /api/health` reports
`"durable": true` once it is configured, and the startup log says `EPHEMERAL`
in capitals when it is not.

An entry arrives from `uv run publish --enter`, from the workshop or a shell,
with the entrant's Hugging Face token (in practice a write token, the one
`publish` uploads with). The Space asks the Hub's whoami-v2 whose token it is,
then drops it: it never stores or logs it. The site keeps Hugging Face OAuth,
scope `openid profile`, for signing in, votes and withdrawing one's own
entries. Entering the board takes a Hugging Face repo the
author published themselves, raced at a pinned revision, and the board's
`.onnx` link resolves straight to that repo. A `.onnx` in hand is raced locally with
`arena score <onnx> --event <id>` and entered with
`uv run publish --onnx … --enter --event <id>`; the site itself has no entry form.

## Social clips

Every published run gets two clips — landscape and vertical — and the Space
renders none of them. The moment a publish completes it launches an HF Job of
its own on its own image, which runs `arena clip <run>`: a headless Chromium
photographs the arena's stage frame by frame on the job's GPU, ffmpeg encodes
the video, and the job writes the clip into the dataset. That is why the image
carries Chromium, ffmpeg and the EGL dispatchers (`libegl1`, `libgles2`).

Measured on 2026-10-05 on a 386-frame sprint clip: 75 s on a **t4-small** job,
against 588 s in SwiftShader on the Space's own eight vCPUs and 553 s on a
sixteen-vCPU job; about a cent a clip. The publication page follows the job,
frame by frame from its log. When the Jobs API refuses a launch, nothing is
rendered elsewhere: the run stays owed — its `clips/<run>/pending.json` marker
is the list — and is launched again later, and at every boot.

| name | kind | value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CHROME` | variable | the browser binary, if not at one of the usual paths |
| `ARENA_CLIPS` | variable | `0` stops owing clips |
| `ARENA_CLIP_FLAVOR` | variable | the job's hardware, default `t4-small` |
| `ARENA_CLIP_NAMESPACE` | variable | the account that runs and pays for the jobs, default the Space's owner |
| `ARENA_CLIP_TOKEN` | secret | the token that launches the jobs, with `job.read` and `job.write` on that account; default `HF_TOKEN`. The jobs themselves write to the dataset with `HF_TOKEN` |
| `ARENA_CLIP_JOBS` | variable | jobs running at once at most, default 4 |
| `ARENA_CLIP_PARALLEL` | variable | layouts a job renders at once, default half its cores |
| `ARENA_CLIP_BACKFILL` | variable | `1` also owes a clip to every run that has none — the log as it stood before clips — newest first, behind fresh publishes; once caught up a boot finds nothing to do |
| `ARENA_ORIGIN` | variable | where the recorder's Chrome loads `clip.html`, if not this server's own loopback address |

Each event's `[clip]` manifest section tunes its framing, duration and sounds
— see `arena/manifest.py`.

To render one run's clips by hand — a historical run, or a retry — run
`arena clip <run_id> --store DIR`; with `ARENA_DATASET` set it writes to the
dataset, as a job does, and `ARENA_CLIP_GPU=1` draws on the machine's GPU.

## Recovering the board

The run log can be lost — without `ARENA_DATASET` and `HF_TOKEN` it lives on a
container filesystem that every redeploy wipes. The **policies** are not lost
with it: publishing writes each one into its author's own public repo, tagged
`microduck-policy` and carrying a `manifest.json`. So the board is re-derivable.

```bash
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board                    # every event
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board --event sprint-2m
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board --all-tagged       # the whole ecosystem
```

With `ARENA_RECOVER=1` the same reconciliation runs at every startup, in a
background thread so it never blocks the Space coming up. It re-races only what
is **missing**, keyed on the Hub revision, so on a durable store it costs one
listing and finds nothing to do — measured: a second pass over a full store
restores 0 runs in 6 s. It is off by default because the local path must keep
working with no account and no network.

Two limits worth knowing. It restores only what reached the Hub — a `Test` run,
or anything published before policies went to the Hub, left nothing to recover.
And times are **re-measured**, never read back: a ranking you cannot re-verify
is not one worth restoring.

One thing this deployment does NOT have yet:

- **Submissions are synchronous and CPU-bound.** One entry is 33 simulated runs
  — about 3 s on a developer laptop, and proportionally longer on a shared
  2-vCPU Space. It works; it is not instant, and there is no queue.

## Run it

Python 3.12 (`uv` installs it: `uv python install 3.12`).

```bash
uv sync
cd app && npm install && npm run build && cd ..
uv run arena serve --store ~/arena-board --user $USER
```

`arena serve` finds the built site in `app/dist`. A wheel of this package (`uv build --wheel`
after `uv run python scripts/bundle_frontend.py`) carries it inside the package instead, at
`arena/frontend/`, so an installed Arena serves its site with nothing else on disk; that is
what the release workflow attaches to a tag. After building a wheel, delete `arena/frontend/`
(`rm -rf arena/frontend`) — an editable install prefers it over every later `npm run build` of
`app/dist`.

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8000>.

The home page is the club: `Season standings` ranks players by the points
their publications earned (first publication on an event 100, each published
run 10 capped at three a day, beating your own best 25 once per event, and
250/150/100 while you hold a podium place), and `Pick your round` lists the
events. The chip top-right opens your page, `#/p/<user>`; the standings link
to everyone else's. Points are folded from the run log on every request, like
the board — `GET /api/standings` and `GET /api/players/<user>`.

## From the command line

```bash
uv run arena events

# The repo vendors one reference policy, so this works with no setup:
REF=arena/assets/policies/BEST_alpha_walking.onnx
uv run arena score $REF --event sprint-2m
uv run arena score $REF --event sprint-2m --user me --name reference --store ~/arena-board
uv run arena board --event sprint-2m --store ~/arena-board

# A stage event plays a command timeline (arena/timeline.py) instead of racing:
uv run arena score $REF --event got-a-talent --timeline timeline.json
```

## What a policy has to be

One ONNX file with a **61-D observation input** and a **14-D action output** — the
same contract `robotd` enforces on the real robot, so a policy the Arena accepts
will load there too. A wrong shape is rejected with the reason:

```
observation width is 51, expected 61
```

## The events

| Event | Rig | Course | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sprint-2m` | legs | 2 m flat | 0.25 m/s forward |
| `roller-sprint-2m` | rollers | 2 m flat | 0.6 m/s forward |
| `hill-climb-1m5` | legs | 1.5 m at 8° | 0.25 m/s forward |

Locally the board shows **one row per policy**, so your own `v1` and `v2` race each other;
resubmitting the same name only improves that row. A deployed multi-user Space sets
`ARENA_RANK_BY=user` to show one row per person instead, and `arena board --rank-by user`
does the same from the command line.

An entry is scored as the **mean finish time over five perturbed starts**, with
any failure to finish counted at the event's time limit — so a policy that is
quick four times and falls once ranks below a steady one. The replay you watch is
the median finishing run, not the best.

Two things about the shipped reference policy are worth knowing before reading
too much into a time: it tracks about 44% of its commanded velocity, and below
roughly 0.2 m/s commanded it does not walk at all. Both are measured; see the
design doc's calibration table.

## Developing

```bash
uv run --extra dev pytest        # engine + API
cd app && npm test               # frontend units
cd app && npm run dev            # UI on :5173, proxying /api to :8000
```

`app/src/rig.js` and the vendored `app/public/robot/` assets come from
[the Microduck sandbox Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator)
at a pinned commit — see `arena/assets/PROVENANCE.md`. Re-vendoring can change
what a policy scores, so `RUNNER_VERSION` in `arena/constants.py` must be bumped
in the same commit.

## Design

- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-03-microduck-arena-design.md` — the design and every decision behind it
- `docs/probe-results.md` — measured cost of an evaluation

# microduck-arena

Race a Microduck policy against every other policy, on a clock you can trust.

New to competing? Read [Train your first policy](docs/guides/train-a-policy.md),
then open **Training & rules** on your chosen challenge.

Submitted policies are evaluated **server-side** on a fixed course over five
perturbed seeds, at every commanded speed in the event's declared sweep, and the
best result is recorded. A time reported by a browser is a number in devtools;
this one reproduces on the Space's hardware (x86_64 Linux), and you can download
any published policy and race it yourself. Elsewhere — a Mac, or another
architecture — the same run gives different numbers: the servo model is chaotic
enough that a run diverges after a few seconds of simulated time, so a local time
is indicative, not the board's.

It runs two ways, and both are first-class:

- **Locally**, with no Hugging Face account, no OAuth and no network. The run log
  is a directory on your disk.
- **As a Space** (this repo is one). Same code path; its times are the
  board's, and a local run on other hardware gives indicative ones.

## Deploying to the Space

The source of truth is the GitHub repo
[`pollen-robotics/microduck-arena`](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck-arena).
**Every push to `main` deploys** — `.github/workflows/deploy-space.yml` publishes
the tree to <https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-arena>.

`git push` to the Hub does not work here: it rejects binary files pushed through
plain git and asks for Xet instead, and this repo vendors a GLB, forty-odd STLs
and an ONNX policy. So the deploy goes through the Hub API, which speaks Xet
natively — the same script the workflow runs is the one to run by hand:

```bash
uv run python scripts/deploy_space.py            # publishes the working tree
uv run python scripts/deploy_space.py --dry-run  # shows what would go
```

The run log is not part of this. It lives in the `ARENA_DATASET` dataset repo,
which a deploy never touches, so the board and the standings survive every
redeploy — see *Running as a Space* below.

The Space rebuilds itself on each upload. Its own Docker build re-measures the
golden run and fails if the physics does not reproduce, so a broken build is
better than a silently wrong leaderboard.

## Releasing

A tag `vX.Y.Z` matching `version` in `pyproject.toml` builds the wheel — package, built site,
meshes — and attaches it to a GitHub release (`.github/workflows/release.yml`). That wheel is
what `microduck-challenges` depends on:

```bash
git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0
```

## Running as a Space

The container filesystem is ephemeral, so a Space needs somewhere durable to
keep the run log. Set two things in **Settings → Variables and secrets**:

| name | kind | value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ARENA_DATASET` | variable | the dataset repo that holds the log, e.g. `pollen-robotics/microduck-arena-runs` |
| `HF_TOKEN` | **secret** | a token with write access to that dataset |

Without both, the Space still boots and the board still works — but every
recorded run is lost the next time it restarts or wakes from sleep. A
published policy's `.onnx` is not at risk from this: it lives in the
publishing author's own Hub repo, not on the Space. `GET /api/health` reports
`"durable": true` once it is configured, and the startup log says `EPHEMERAL`
in capitals when it is not.

An entry arrives from `uv run publish --enter`, from the workshop or a shell,
with the entrant's Hugging Face token (in practice a write token, the one
`publish` uploads with). The Space asks the Hub's whoami-v2 whose token it is,
then drops it: it never stores or logs it. The site keeps Hugging Face OAuth,
scope `openid profile`, for signing in, votes and withdrawing one's own
entries. Entering the board takes a Hugging Face repo the
author published themselves, raced at a pinned revision, and the board's
`.onnx` link resolves straight to that repo. A `.onnx` in hand is raced locally with
`arena score <onnx> --event <id>` and entered with
`uv run publish --onnx … --enter --event <id>`; the site itself has no entry form.

## Social clips

Every published run gets two clips — landscape and vertical — and the Space
renders none of them. The moment a publish completes it launches an HF Job of
its own on its own image, which runs `arena clip <run>`: a headless Chromium
photographs the arena's stage frame by frame on the job's GPU, ffmpeg encodes
the video, and the job writes the clip into the dataset. That is why the image
carries Chromium, ffmpeg and the EGL dispatchers (`libegl1`, `libgles2`).

Measured on 2026-10-05 on a 386-frame sprint clip: 75 s on a **t4-small** job,
against 588 s in SwiftShader on the Space's own eight vCPUs and 553 s on a
sixteen-vCPU job; about a cent a clip. The publication page follows the job,
frame by frame from its log. When the Jobs API refuses a launch, nothing is
rendered elsewhere: the run stays owed — its `clips/<run>/pending.json` marker
is the list — and is launched again later, and at every boot.

| name | kind | value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CHROME` | variable | the browser binary, if not at one of the usual paths |
| `ARENA_CLIPS` | variable | `0` stops owing clips |
| `ARENA_CLIP_FLAVOR` | variable | the job's hardware, default `t4-small` |
| `ARENA_CLIP_NAMESPACE` | variable | the account that runs and pays for the jobs, default the Space's owner |
| `ARENA_CLIP_TOKEN` | secret | the token that launches the jobs, with `job.read` and `job.write` on that account; default `HF_TOKEN`. The jobs themselves write to the dataset with `HF_TOKEN` |
| `ARENA_CLIP_JOBS` | variable | jobs running at once at most, default 4 |
| `ARENA_CLIP_PARALLEL` | variable | layouts a job renders at once, default half its cores |
| `ARENA_CLIP_BACKFILL` | variable | `1` also owes a clip to every run that has none — the log as it stood before clips — newest first, behind fresh publishes; once caught up a boot finds nothing to do |
| `ARENA_ORIGIN` | variable | where the recorder's Chrome loads `clip.html`, if not this server's own loopback address |

Each event's `[clip]` manifest section tunes its framing, duration and sounds
— see `arena/manifest.py`.

To render one run's clips by hand — a historical run, or a retry — run
`arena clip <run_id> --store DIR`; with `ARENA_DATASET` set it writes to the
dataset, as a job does, and `ARENA_CLIP_GPU=1` draws on the machine's GPU.

## Recovering the board

The run log can be lost — without `ARENA_DATASET` and `HF_TOKEN` it lives on a
container filesystem that every redeploy wipes. The **policies** are not lost
with it: publishing writes each one into its author's own public repo, tagged
`microduck-policy` and carrying a `manifest.json`. So the board is re-derivable.

```bash
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board                    # every event
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board --event sprint-2m
uv run arena recover --store ~/arena-board --all-tagged       # the whole ecosystem
```

With `ARENA_RECOVER=1` the same reconciliation runs at every startup, in a
background thread so it never blocks the Space coming up. It re-races only what
is **missing**, keyed on the Hub revision, so on a durable store it costs one
listing and finds nothing to do — measured: a second pass over a full store
restores 0 runs in 6 s. It is off by default because the local path must keep
working with no account and no network.

Two limits worth knowing. It restores only what reached the Hub — a `Test` run,
or anything published before policies went to the Hub, left nothing to recover.
And times are **re-measured**, never read back: a ranking you cannot re-verify
is not one worth restoring.

One thing this deployment does NOT have yet:

- **Submissions are synchronous and CPU-bound.** One entry is 33 simulated runs
  — about 3 s on a developer laptop, and proportionally longer on a shared
  2-vCPU Space. It works; it is not instant, and there is no queue.

## Run it

Python 3.12 (`uv` installs it: `uv python install 3.12`).

```bash
uv sync
cd app && npm install && npm run build && cd ..
uv run arena serve --store ~/arena-board --user $USER
```

`arena serve` finds the built site in `app/dist`. A wheel of this package (`uv build --wheel`
after `uv run python scripts/bundle_frontend.py`) carries it inside the package instead, at
`arena/frontend/`, so an installed Arena serves its site with nothing else on disk; that is
what the release workflow attaches to a tag. After building a wheel, delete `arena/frontend/`
(`rm -rf arena/frontend`) — an editable install prefers it over every later `npm run build` of
`app/dist`.

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8000>.

The home page is the club: `Season standings` ranks players by the points
their publications earned (first publication on an event 100, each published
run 10 capped at three a day, beating your own best 25 once per event, and
250/150/100 while you hold a podium place), and `Pick your round` lists the
events. The chip top-right opens your page, `#/p/<user>`; the standings link
to everyone else's. Points are folded from the run log on every request, like
the board — `GET /api/standings` and `GET /api/players/<user>`.

## From the command line

```bash
uv run arena events

# The repo vendors one reference policy, so this works with no setup:
REF=arena/assets/policies/BEST_alpha_walking.onnx
uv run arena score $REF --event sprint-2m
uv run arena score $REF --event sprint-2m --user me --name reference --store ~/arena-board
uv run arena board --event sprint-2m --store ~/arena-board

# A stage event plays a command timeline (arena/timeline.py) instead of racing:
uv run arena score $REF --event got-a-talent --timeline timeline.json
```

## What a policy has to be

One ONNX file with a **61-D observation input** and a **14-D action output** — the
same contract `robotd` enforces on the real robot, so a policy the Arena accepts
will load there too. A wrong shape is rejected with the reason:

```
observation width is 51, expected 61
```

## The events

| Event | Rig | Course | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sprint-2m` | legs | 2 m flat | 0.25 m/s forward |
| `roller-sprint-2m` | rollers | 2 m flat | 0.6 m/s forward |
| `hill-climb-1m5` | legs | 1.5 m at 8° | 0.25 m/s forward |

Locally the board shows **one row per policy**, so your own `v1` and `v2` race each other;
resubmitting the same name only improves that row. A deployed multi-user Space sets
`ARENA_RANK_BY=user` to show one row per person instead, and `arena board --rank-by user`
does the same from the command line.

An entry is scored as the **mean finish time over five perturbed starts**, with
any failure to finish counted at the event's time limit — so a policy that is
quick four times and falls once ranks below a steady one. The replay you watch is
the median finishing run, not the best.

Two things about the shipped reference policy are worth knowing before reading
too much into a time: it tracks about 44% of its commanded velocity, and below
roughly 0.2 m/s commanded it does not walk at all. Both are measured; see the
design doc's calibration table.

## Developing

```bash
uv run --extra dev pytest        # engine + API
cd app && npm test               # frontend units
cd app && npm run dev            # UI on :5173, proxying /api to :8000
```

`app/src/rig.js` and the vendored `app/public/robot/` assets come from
[the Microduck sandbox Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator)
at a pinned commit — see `arena/assets/PROVENANCE.md`. Re-vendoring can change
what a policy scores, so `RUNNER_VERSION` in `arena/constants.py` must be bumped
in the same commit.

## Design

- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-03-microduck-arena-design.md` — the design and every decision behind it
- `docs/probe-results.md` — measured cost of an evaluation

record.author: masterjedi1337
record.body:
Click-to-walk waypoint control  (runtime only, no new policy)

Left-click a point on the arena floor and the duck walks (or skates) there. The click is turned into the same [vx, 0, wz] twist command the locomotion policies already track, so no retraining is involved. Works in both variants: legs and rollers.

How it works
- New WaypointSource (app/src/game/controls/waypoint.js) raycasts the click onto the floor plane, clamps the target inside the arena, then steers each frame: proportional yaw toward the target, forward speed scaled by cos(heading error) so the duck turns in place first, commands EMA-smoothed and clamped to the trained velocity limits. A 0.12 m dead zone stops it on arrival (all-zero command = trained "stand still").
- Click vs. drag disambiguation: a target only arms on a short, low-movement mouse press, so camera orbit and duck/ball grab-drags are untouched. Suppressed in head mode, during roll/kick actions, while grabbing, or when input is locked.
- Arbitration: registered last in the controller's source list, so keyboard/gamepad/touch preempt it instantly, and any manual input cancels the pending target (no snap-back to a stale click). Sim reset also cancels it.
- Feedback: a pulsing orange ring marks the active target; the cursor shows a crosshair over clickable floor.
- Small refactor: trunk-yaw-from-quaternion extraction now shared as duckYaw() in game.js (chase cam, camera reset, and the waypoint follower all use it).

Tested manually in both leg (walking) and roller (skating) variants.

record.author: ramzi-abbyad
record.body:
I've been experimenting with an optional adapter that lets a script drive the browser simulator using the physical duck's JSON-RPC API.

The idea is to try routines with a virtual duck first - choreography, demos, or teaching exercises - and reuse the supported commands when working with hardware. You can develop the simulator side without a physical duck connected.

The prototype currently supports robot.move, robot.stop, and robot.do for ground pick, left/right kicks, sit/stand, and roulade. Commands pass through a local gateway into the simulator's existing input controller, so its trained policies and MuJoCo physics handle the movement. API movement expires after 500 ms without an update, and robot.stop releases API control immediately.

There's also a simulator-only robot.get_state method for checking readiness, locomotion mode, and active skills. This is still a partial implementation of the robot API, and transferring a routine to hardware needs separate testing.

The implementation is on the adapter-v2 branch, including the latest forward-movement fix. These links show the code, the changes from the upstream revision it started from, and how to run it locally:

- [Adapter branch](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/tree/adapter-v2)
- [Implementation diff](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/compare/e81974b932c7ca1819843b7bb3dcd42e2993e98e...3f0b2cca0632a636ca534e1bb50767eae8ba3c5f)
- [Design and local run instructions](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/blob/adapter-v2/docs/adapter-architecture.md)

The current checks include 31 passing automated tests and a headless-browser run that verified forward displacement, stop handling, and launching a kick through the gateway. The gateway binds to localhost by default and currently has no authentication, so it's for local use.

Would this be useful in the official simulator? I'd appreciate your thoughts on:

1. Whether you'd prefer an optional integration here in the Space or a separate adapter package.
2. Whether simulator state should follow robot.subscribe / robot.state, and any other API or safety details to align.
3. What license applies to downstream use of the simulator source.

If there's interest, I'd be happy to prepare a focused PR.

I've been experimenting with an optional adapter that lets a script drive the browser simulator using the physical duck's JSON-RPC API.

The idea is to try routines with a virtual duck first - choreography, demos, or teaching exercises - and reuse the supported commands when working with hardware. You can develop the simulator side without a physical duck connected.

The prototype currently supports robot.move, robot.stop, and robot.do for ground pick, left/right kicks, sit/stand, and roulade. Commands pass through a local gateway into the simulator's existing input controller, so its trained policies and MuJoCo physics handle the movement. API movement expires after 500 ms without an update, and robot.stop releases API control immediately.

There's also a simulator-only robot.get_state method for checking readiness, locomotion mode, and active skills. This is still a partial implementation of the robot API, and transferring a routine to hardware needs separate testing.

The implementation is on the adapter-v2 branch, including the latest forward-movement fix. These links show the code, the changes from the upstream revision it started from, and how to run it locally:

- [Adapter branch](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/tree/adapter-v2)
- [Implementation diff](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/compare/e81974b932c7ca1819843b7bb3dcd42e2993e98e...3f0b2cca0632a636ca534e1bb50767eae8ba3c5f)
- [Design and local run instructions](https://github.com/ramziabbyad1/microduck-sim-bridge/blob/adapter-v2/docs/adapter-architecture.md)

The current checks include 31 passing automated tests and a headless-browser run that verified forward displacement, stop handling, and launching a kick through the gateway. The gateway binds to localhost by default and currently has no authentication, so it's for local use.

Would this be useful in the official simulator? I'd appreciate your thoughts on:

1. Whether you'd prefer an optional integration here in the Space or a separate adapter package.
2. Whether simulator state should follow robot.subscribe / robot.state, and any other API or safety details to align.
3. What license applies to downstream use of the simulator source.

If there's interest, I'd be happy to prepare a focused PR.

# Microduck RL playground

Real trained RL policies for the Microduck robot, running fully in the
browser: MuJoCo compiled to WebAssembly steps the physics, onnxruntime-web
runs the policy network at 50 Hz. No server, no backend.

Two locomotion variants of the same robot are included: **legs** (walking,
the default) and **rollers** (the wheeled skating variant). Press `M` (or
hold D-pad up ~1 s on a gamepad) to switch; the roller model, meshes and
policies are lazy-loaded on the first switch.

## Policies

| Mode | Checkpoint | What it does |
|--------|-----------|--------------|
| Run (legs) | `BEST_alpha_walking.onnx` | Velocity-tracking locomotion (arrows / WASD to steer) |
| Sit | `BEST_alpha_sitstand.onnx` | Sits down on its hull, stands back up |
| Roll | `roulade.onnx` | Rolls over and recovers |
| Kick | `ball_kick_left.onnx` / `ball_kick_right.onnx` | Blind one-shot kick (0.5 s window, zeroed commands), left or right leg |
| Drive (rollers) | `BEST_roller.onnx` | Velocity-tracking skating on 4 passive wheels (higher top speed: 0.6 m/s) |
| Crouch (rollers) | `BEST_roller_crouch.onnx` | One-shot crouch-glide: sinks low over ~3.5 s and stands back up (phase-encoded command) |

Policies and MJCF model from
[pollen-robotics/microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck)
and [pollen-robotics/microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl).

## Controls

- Arrows or WASD / ZQSD: forward / back + turn
- M: switch legs <-> rollers
- Q / E (A / E on AZERTY): kick left / right (legs only)
- F: alternate left / right kicks (legs only)
- R: sit / stand (legs) / crouch-glide (rollers)
- G: ground pick (legs only)
- C: toggle the chase camera (on by default; dragging detaches it)
- Space: reset
- Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom
- Colour dots: repaint the duck (it quacks)

In roller mode the legs-only actions (kicks, sit) are disabled and their
hints fade out; play the ball by driving into it.

### URL parameters

- `?boot=1`: skip the welcome modal and land straight on the BIOS console,
  which then shows the real loading progress live (honest loader) before
  the normal entrance plays. Boot failures (missing asset, policy fetch
  error...) freeze the console on a `SYSTEM HALTED` screen with the error
  detail - handy for debugging.

The ball's physics are local to your tab, but its pose is broadcast with
your duck's, so other visitors see a translucent copy of your ball next
to your ghost (and you see theirs). A square arena (3 x 3 m) fences the
play area so neither the ball nor the duck can wander off.

### Gamepad

Plug in a controller and the same mapping as the real robot runtime applies:

- Left stick: forward / back + turn
- Right stick: orbit the camera (detaches the chase cam)
- R3 (right stick click): toggle the chase cam back on
- X or D-pad down: sit / stand (legs) / crouch-glide (rollers)
- A: ground pick (legs only)
- Y: toggle head control
- RB / LB: right / left kick (legs only)
- D-pad up: hold ~1 s to switch legs <-> rollers (the real robot uses a 3 s hold)
- Right trigger: mouth (analog) + quack
- Left trigger: hold for wheee
- A: enter / resume the game while the title or pause overlay is up
- Menu/Start (or Select): exit back to the title overlay while in-game

## Multiplayer ghosts

Other people visiting the Space at the same time show up as translucent
ducks, live. Peer-to-peer WebRTC via [Trystero](https://github.com/dmotz/trystero)
(serverless signaling over public Nostr relays), so it works from a static
Space with no backend. Each tab broadcasts its duck's pose (trunk + 14
joints + jaw + colour + locomotion variant) at 10 Hz; up to 3 ghosts are
rendered, extra peers stay connected but invisible. The camcorder-style OSD
in the top-right corner shows "N ONLINE" when peers are around.

Ghost limitations in v1: a peer in roller mode renders with the roller rig
only if your tab has already loaded it (otherwise it falls back to the leg
rig), and ghost wheels don't spin (passive wheel joints aren't broadcast).
Old clients simply ignore the new variant flag.

## How it works

The app is a Vite + React + MUI shell around an imperative game core:
React/MUI renders the UI chrome (title menu, BIOS console, HUD, touch
overlay), react-three-fiber owns the canvas/lights/environment, and the
physics/policy/rig loop lives in framework-agnostic modules under
`app/src/game/`. A zustand store bridges the two (game state out,
UI intents in).

- `app/src/game/game.js` fetches the MJCF (`robot_allcollisions.xml`, or
  `robot_allcollisions_rollers.xml` for the roller variant), strips the
  visual geoms, injects a floor, arena walls, a ball, a collision box for
  the arcade cabinet row and a STAND keyframe, and compiles it with the
  official `@mujoco/mujoco` WASM bindings.
- Both variants share the exact same policy interface: 61D observation
  (gyro, projected gravity, 14 joint pos/vel, last action, 13D command)
  and 14 position-targets, matching [`microduck_rl/scripts/infer_policy.py`](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl/blob/main/scripts/infer_policy.py).
  The roller variant adds 4 passive wheel hinges that appear in `qpos`
  (zeroed in the keyframe) but not in the observation.
- Rendering is a three.js rig built from `kinematics.json` /
  `kinematics_rollers.json` + decimated STL meshes, driven directly from
  MuJoCo `qpos` (including the passive wheel spin).
- Switching variants swaps the compiled model + data + rig + ONNX sessions
  wholesale; both stay resident after the first load so toggling back and
  forth is instant.

## Development

Large binary assets (robot meshes, GLB models, ONNX policies) are stored
with [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com/). Clone with LFS installed, or pull
the real files after a plain clone - otherwise the app boots against
text pointer files and fails with errors like
`SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'v', "version ht"... is not valid JSON`
(that string is the start of an LFS pointer, not your model):

```bash
git lfs install   # once per machine
git lfs pull      # fetch the actual binaries in an existing clone
```

```bash
cd app
npm install
npm run dev     # dev server on http://localhost:5173
npm run build   # production bundle in app/dist/
```

The Space builds with the included `Dockerfile` (Vite build, served by
nginx-unprivileged on port 8080). Static assets (meshes, policies, audio,
images) live in `app/public/` and keep their historical URLs.

## License

The app code is released under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE).
